title: SHOULD CHRISTIANS CELEBRATE HALLOWEEN?
paragraphs: SHOULD CHRISTIANS CELEBRATE HALLOWEEN?
The question is not whether you can wear the costume, carve the pumpkin, or take the candy. The question is whether Jesus can be Lord of what you are about to do.
The porch light is on.
There is a plastic skeleton hanging from somebody’s tree.
Children are running down the sidewalk dressed like superheroes, princesses, monsters, ghosts, witches, and characters they saw in movies.
Someone is laughing.
Someone is handing out candy.
Someone at church has already posted that Halloween is demonic.
Someone else has already responded that Christians need to stop being legalistic.
And somewhere between the shouting, the costumes, the church harvest festivals, the haunted houses, the candy bowls, the arguments about paganism, and the social-media debates...
a sincere Christian is sitting quietly with a question that deserves more than a meme.
“Jesus... what do You want me to do?”
That question changes everything.
Because perhaps the most dangerous thing about the Halloween debate is that we can become so obsessed with proving which Christians are wrong that we forget to ask whether Christ is being glorified.
So before you defend Halloween...
before you condemn everyone who participates...
before you call another believer compromised...
before you call another believer legalistic...
put down the argument for a moment.
Put Jesus in the center.
And ask the question that reaches much deeper than October 31:
Can I bring Christ into what I am doing without asking Him to wait outside?
Because Christianity was never supposed to be a game of discovering how close we can stand to darkness without technically sinning.
It is a life surrendered to Jesus Christ.
And that means we have to begin where Scripture begins.
Not with superstition.
Not with internet folklore.
Not with fear.
Not with nostalgia.
Not with “My family has always done it.”
Not even with “My church says...”
With the Word of God.
Here is something Christians on both sides of this argument need the humility to admit:
The Bible never mentions Halloween by name.
There is no verse that says, “Thou shalt not celebrate Halloween.”
There is also no verse declaring October 31 spiritually harmless and giving Christians permission to participate in absolutely anything associated with it.
That means we must not manufacture a commandment God did not give.
But it also means we cannot use the absence of the word “Halloween” as permission to ignore commandments God most certainly did give.
And some of those commandments are unmistakable.
God told Israel:
“Let there not be found among you anyone... who practices divination... engages in witchcraft... casts spells, or who is a medium or spiritist or who consults the dead.”
That is the substance of Deuteronomy 18:10–12.
This is not ambiguous.
The Hebrew vocabulary in this passage describes actual occult practices—divination, sorcery, spell-casting, mediums, and seeking information from the dead.
God's objection was not to children eating chocolate.
It was not to the color orange.
It was not to pumpkins.
It was not to October.
It was to human beings seeking supernatural power, revelation, guidance, or communion apart from Him.
That distinction matters enormously.
Because biblical discernment refuses two opposite errors.
It refuses to call darkness light.
But it also refuses to invent darkness where Scripture has not called something darkness.
A plastic spider is not a demon.
A piece of candy is not witchcraft.
A child wearing a firefighter costume has not performed necromancy.
At the same time, actual occultism does not become innocent simply because somebody calls it entertainment.
God does not become comfortable with divination because we put decorations around it.
He does not approve of attempting to contact the dead because it happens at a party.
He does not suddenly bless spells, séances, occult rituals, spiritism, or attempts to obtain supernatural power outside of Him because someone says, “Relax. We're just having fun.”
Scripture gives Christians a real boundary.
Paul writes:
Ephesians 5:11.
The Greek is striking:
καὶ μὴ συγκοινωνεῖτε τοῖς ἔργοις τοῖς ἀκάρποις τοῦ σκότους
Kai mē synkoinōneite tois ergois tois akarpois tou skotous.
The important word is συγκοινωνεῖτε — synkoinōneite.
It carries the idea of sharing in, participating with, or becoming a partner in something.
Paul is not teaching Christians to panic whenever darkness exists around them.
If that were the command, Christians could never enter a broken world.
Jesus Himself ate with sinners.
He walked among people religious society had rejected.
He touched the unclean.
He stepped directly into human misery.
But He never participated in their darkness in order to reach them.
He brought light into it.
That difference may be the heart of the entire Halloween question.
There is a difference between being present where darkness exists and participating in darkness.
Read that again.
Because this is where the conversation becomes uncomfortable for everyone.
The Christian who says, “Everything associated with Halloween is automatically demonic,” must be careful not to create a universal biblical prohibition where Scripture itself has not stated one.
But the Christian who says, “It's just fun; none of it matters,” has another problem.
For a follower of Jesus, nothing belongs in a category called “Jesus doesn't matter here.”
Not our entertainment.
Not our sexuality.
Not our money.
Not our humor.
Not our relationships.
Not our screens.
Not our traditions.
Not our holidays.
Paul gives us a breathtakingly simple test:
“Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God.”
1 Corinthians 10:31.
And in Greek:
πάντα εἰς δόξαν θεοῦ ποιεῖτε
Panta eis doxan Theou poieite.
Do everything toward the glory of God.
Suddenly the question is no longer merely:
“Is Halloween allowed?”
Now it becomes:
“Can what I am doing honestly be directed toward the glory of God?”
That is harder.
Because rules can sometimes be manipulated.
Love for Christ cannot.
Imagine Jesus physically standing beside you on October 31.
Not angry.
Not waiting to catch you.
Just present.
The Jesus who was scourged for you.
The Jesus whose hands were pierced for you.
The Jesus who carried your shame to Calvary.
The Jesus who walked out of the grave.
The Jesus you call Lord.
Would His presence make you uncomfortable with what you planned to do?
Would you change the costume?
Turn off the movie?
Leave the party?
Avoid the occult-themed attraction?
Stop joking about something you suddenly realized should not be entertainment?
Or would you gladly say:
“Lord, stay with me. I want You here.”
That is not legalism.
That is relationship.
And there is another side Christians cannot ignore.
Romans 14 deals with believers disagreeing about matters involving food and the observance of days.
Paul writes:
Then comes an important phrase:
ὁ φρονῶν τὴν ἡμέραν κυρίῳ φρονεῖ
Ho phronōn tēn hēmeran Kyriō phronei.
The one regarding the day regards it to the Lord.
Paul's concern is not careless relativism.
He does not say sin becomes holy when your conscience approves it.
Elsewhere Scripture clearly identifies behavior Christians cannot baptize with personal preference.
You cannot say, “My conscience is fine with adultery.”
You cannot say, “My conscience is comfortable with idolatry.”
You cannot say, “Sorcery doesn't bother me personally.”
God's explicit commands remain God's commands.
But where Scripture leaves room for conscience, Christians should be extremely careful about climbing onto God's throne and issuing universal commandments in His name.
Paul goes even further:
“Why dost thou judge thy brother? or why dost thou set at nought thy brother?”
Romans 14:10.
That should make both camps uncomfortable.
Maybe that is good.
Because perhaps some Christians need to repent of participating in darkness.
And perhaps others need to repent of the pride with which they condemn brothers and sisters whose conduct Scripture itself does not explicitly condemn.
Conviction without love becomes cruelty.
Freedom without holiness becomes compromise.
Truth without humility becomes a weapon.
And grace without truth becomes permission.
Jesus offers something better than all four.
Truth and grace.
So should Christians celebrate Halloween?
The most biblically responsible answer requires more precision than a slogan.

A Christian should not participate in actual occult practices, divination, séances, spell-casting, attempts to contact spirits or the dead, or anything else Scripture explicitly identifies as forbidden spiritual practice.
That boundary is not negotiable simply because October 31 makes such imagery culturally popular.

Beyond those explicit boundaries, believers must examine what they are actually doing, why they are doing it, what it celebrates, what effect it has on their conscience, what it communicates to others, and whether they can genuinely offer it to Christ.
One Christian family may decide:
“We want nothing to do with Halloween. We will spend the evening differently.”
They should be free to honor Christ that way.

Another Christian family may hand candy to neighborhood children, meet parents on their street, show hospitality, give out Scripture cards, host a church gathering, or use an evening when neighbors unexpectedly arrive at their door as an opportunity to demonstrate unusual kindness.
They should not automatically be accused of worshiping demons because they handed a child a chocolate bar.
Another believer may have come out of actual occultism.
For that person, symbols other people consider harmless may carry memories, temptations, associations, and spiritual wounds others do not understand.
Love says:
I will not mock your conscience.
Another believer may have never practiced occultism at all and may see costumes and candy simply as neighborhood fun.
Love says:
I will not invent secret motives in your heart.
Romans 14 calls us toward conviction without contempt.
And that may be exactly what the modern Church desperately needs.
Because while Christians fight about pumpkins...
people are dying without Christ.
While we attack each other over costumes...
marriages are collapsing.
Teenagers are quietly wondering whether life is worth living.
Pornography is discipling millions behind locked doors.
Parents are exhausted.
Believers are secretly addicted.
Churchgoers are smiling on Sunday and crying alone at night.
People who know Christian vocabulary still do not know the Christ who makes dead people alive.
Maybe October 31 is not merely a battlefield to escape.
Maybe for some believers it can become a mission field.
Not by pretending darkness is light.
But by doing what Christians have always been called to do:
carry light into darkness.
Jesus said:
“I am the light of the world.”
And here is where this stops being an article about Halloween.
Because there is a darkness far more dangerous than any haunted house.
It is the darkness inside us.
We are extraordinarily good at spotting darkness when somebody decorates their front yard with it.
We are much less comfortable confronting the darkness we hide behind our own front door.
The bitterness nobody knows about.
The pornography deleted from the browser history.
The affair living inside text messages.
The envy behind the smile.
The resentment toward someone at church.
The addiction.
The secret account.
The unforgiveness.
The pride disguised as discernment.
The judgment disguised as holiness.
The compromise disguised as freedom.
Maybe you came here asking whether Christians should celebrate Halloween.
And somehow Jesus turned the question around.
“What are you allowing in your heart?”
Because you can refuse Halloween completely...
and still entertain darkness every night on your phone.
You can throw every horror movie away...
and still hate your brother.
You can refuse to put a pumpkin outside your house...
while hiding pornography inside it.
You can warn everybody about witches...
while worshiping money.
You can expose the darkness in culture...
while protecting the darkness in yourself.
And suddenly the costume is gone.
The argument is gone.
The Facebook debate is gone.
It is just you.
And Jesus.
And the thing you hoped nobody would mention.
This is where religion often tells you to clean yourself up.
Jesus did something far more astonishing.
He came looking for sinners.
“For the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost.”
Luke 19:10.
He did not wait for scandalous people to become respectable enough to approach Him.
He approached them.
The sexually broken.
The greedy.
The dishonest.
The ashamed.
The religious hypocrite.
The social outcast.
The person everybody else had already reduced to their worst chapter.
Jesus walked into human scandal carrying grace.
Not cheap grace.
Not grace that calls evil good.
Grace that forgives the sinner and then calls the sinner into a new life.
That is the Gospel.
Not:
“Become good enough and maybe God will accept you.”
But:
You sinned.
You could not rescue yourself.
Christ came.
Christ lived without sin.
Christ died for sinners.
Christ was buried.
Christ rose again.
And the risen Jesus still saves people who come to Him in repentance and faith.
Your greatest problem was never October 31.
Your greatest problem was sin.
And your greatest hope is not avoiding a holiday.
Your greatest hope is Jesus Christ.
Maybe the Holy Spirit is putting His finger on something right now that has nothing to do with Halloween.
Something hidden.
Something you have defended for years.
Something you keep renaming because calling it what Scripture calls it would mean you have to surrender it.
Do not run.
Conviction is not Christ pushing you away.
The Gospel is Christ calling sinners out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
You do not have to pretend anymore.
Not because typing those words saves you.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes confession begins when somebody finally stops pretending.
Someone reading beneath you may need to discover that they are not the only believer fighting a battle nobody sees.
Let the Body of Christ behave like a body.
Let believers pray for believers.
Let testimonies meet wounds.
Let grace interrupt shame.
And before you leave this article, ask yourself one final question about Halloween—and about everything else:
Can I thank Jesus for this, invite Jesus into this, and do this for the glory of Jesus?
If the answer is no, do not spend your life hunting for technical loopholes.
You already have your answer.
If Scripture explicitly forbids it, walk away.
If your conscience condemns your participation, do not violate your conscience.
If something is mastering you, surrender it.
If your freedom is damaging someone you should love, consider whether love is asking you to lay that freedom down.
And where faithful Christians reach different conclusions on matters Scripture does not explicitly prohibit, refuse the temptation to become someone else's Holy Spirit.
Be holy.
Be humble.
Be discerning.
Be gracious.
And above everything...
belong completely to Jesus.
You may need these questions again long after the decorations disappear.
Send it privately to the friend who is searching for Christ.
Scripture teaches willing, purposeful generosity—not spiritual transactions.
Supporting Gospel work can be one way a believer chooses to glorify God with his or her resources, but the glory belongs to God, not to the payment.
Give Christ your heart again.
Not the polished version.
Not the Sunday version.
Not the version wearing the Christian costume.
The real one.
The wounded one.
The tempted one.
The ashamed one.
The confused one.
The one still carrying things nobody else knows.
Bring that person to Jesus.
Because Christianity is not ultimately about being the person who successfully avoided every cultural controversy.
It is about belonging to the One who entered our darkness and brought us into His light.
Halloween will come and go.
The costumes will be packed away.
The candy will disappear.
The arguments will move to something else.
But Jesus will still be standing at the center of the question that matters most:
Who has your heart?
And perhaps that is the line worth carrying with you long after October ends:
Do not become so busy identifying the darkness around you that you refuse to let Jesus illuminate the darkness within you.
And whatever you decide about October 31...
do not merely ask whether a Christian can do it.
Ask whether you can place it at the feet of the crucified and risen Christ and sincerely say, “Jesus, this is for Your glory.”
Because the goal was never merely to survive the darkness.
It was to belong to the Light.
